chunks: What transmission line theory is. The question: What is TL theory? Why is it needed?
Transmission line theory is circuit theory for wires that are "electrically long". Normally we treat a wire as one point with the same voltage everywhere.
That works only while signals change slowly compared with their travel time along it. With fast edges, a signal travels as a wave, and the wire can reflect part of it back.
Hold one end of a long rope and flick it. A wave runs down the rope. The far end does not move until the wave arrives, and there the wave can bounce back.
A short rope flicked slowly moves as one piece. A fast signal on a long trace is the flick. The electrical wave also needs a nearby return conductor.
The dashed line is what a lumped wire model predicts. The real far-end voltage arrives 1 nanoseconds late, jumps to 5. 5 volts (67% above the 3. 3 volts supply!)
, then rings around 3. 3 volts with a 4 nanoseconds period (four line delays). The overshoot is exactly why TL analysis is needed: a lumped model never predicts it.
Propagation delay: the time a signal takes to travel along a wire.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the ratio of voltage to current in a wave traveling along the line ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Reflection: part of a wave bouncing back where the line changes ("Reflections and why they matter").
Electrically long: long enough that its delay matters compared with the signal's edge time ("When transmission line analysis applies").
Return path: the second conductor, usually a ground plane, that carries the current back.
On a typical circuit board, signals move about 5. 9 picoseconds per mm, so a 15 cm trace has a delay of about 0. 9 nanoseconds. Send a 1 nanoseconds edge down it.
The driver end is still rising when the front reaches the far end, so the two ends see different voltages and "one voltage everywhere" fails.
A common rule of thumb treats a trace as a transmission line when its delay exceeds about one sixth of the edge time.
For 1 nanoseconds edges, that is any trace longer than about 3 cm. That is the whole idea: fast edges make wires behave as waves.
"Transmission line theory models a wire as distributed series inductance and shunt capacitance, because signals take real time to travel along it.
That gives a characteristic impedance Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' , a propagation delay, and reflections wherever impedance changes, with equals (Z L-Z 0) over (Z L plus Z 0) .

We need it when the trace delay is a meaningful fraction of the signal's rise time, because then ordinary node-voltage analysis fails and you get ringing and overshoot unless you control impedance and terminate."
Quick check. Why can an ordinary wire not be treated as a single node when edges are fast enough?
